title: Polyglot SDK Cutover & Rollback: Adaptive Fetch + Streaming Compatibility Spec
creator: Sana Patel
description: Problem: We are introducing a new adaptive fetch surface that blends cursor-based pagination, resumable streaming, and automatic retry semantics across Python/TS/Go SDKs. Customers must be able to cut over to the new surface with minimal application changes and a clear rollback path in case of regressions. This ticket captures product requirements, acceptance criteria, migration and rollback controls, and cross-team responsibilities for the cutover. The goal is a single behavioral contract per language that preserves existing compatibility guarantees while enabling: adaptive page sizes, resumable event streams (server-ordered chunks + idempotency token), and monitored fallback to legacy endpoints. This PRD is intentionally focused on behavioral guarantees and acceptance criteria rather than implementation details (which will be in ENG subtasks).
requirements: 1) Single fetch primitive per language: provide a unified client method (e.g., client.fetchStream) that supports both paginated and streaming workloads via flags/modes.
2) Backwards compatibility: existing calls using current pagination tokens and stream iterators must continue to work without code changes for at least 6 months after launch.
3) Resumable streams: SDKs must expose a stable resume token format and helper utilities to persist/restore stream position across restarts.
4) Adaptive pagination: client must be able to request an adaptive page size with a hint (min,max) and receive server-provided page-size feedback header for runtime tuning.
5) Retry and idempotency: retries on transient errors should be automatic for idempotent fetches; SDK to expose a configurable retry policy and an idempotency-key helper for non-idempotent flows.
6) Language idioms: Python async iterator, TypeScript AsyncIterable and Node readable stream shim, Go channel + context-aware iterator — each idiom must feel native while matching core behavior.
7) Feature flags & rollout controls: server-side flagging to enable adaptive mode per account; SDK should surface a safe fallback when server indicates feature not ready.
8) Observability hooks: SDK must emit event tracing hooks (start/end/failure/resume) and expose short-lifecycle metrics for token fetch latency, resume success rate, and page-size changes.
9) Controlled rollback: ability to opt-out per-client via environment variable (REDWOOD_SDK_ADAPTIVE_FETCH=off) and a server-side compatibility header that forces legacy semantics.
10) Documentation: migration guide, code examples in Python/TS/Go, deprecation timeline, and snippet for persisting resume tokens.
acceptance_criteria: A1: Behavior parity tests: For 100 representative paginated API calls, SDK responses match legacy client output (order and content) when adaptive mode is disabled.

A2: Resume correctness: Restarting the client and providing a persisted resume token must continue the stream with no duplicates or missing items for >= 99.99% of test cases in our integration harness.
A3: Token compatibility: New resume token can be round-tripped by server and SDK while older tokens remain valid for the deprecation window.
A4: Language-specific ergonomics: Each SDK has idiomatic examples in the README and one end-to-end sample app that uses streaming+resume; approved by DX lead.
A5: Rollback test: With REDWOOD_SDK_ADAPTIVE_FETCH=off, SDK must exhibit legacy pagination behavior in all languages within a single process restart window.
A6: Metrics and tracing: Demo dashboard shows resume rate, average page size, and retry counts for a canary org over 72 hours; alerts configured for resume-fail-rate > 0.5%.
A7: Performance guardrails: Enabling adaptive mode must not increase median request latency by more than 10% for typical 512-token workloads during canary.
A8: Docs & migration: Migration guide reviewed and approved; at least two customer-facing exemplar integrations available for review.
A9: Security: SDK does not persist resume tokens to world-readable locations; review completed by security and any storage recommendations applied.
A10: Release gating: Engineering ambiguity/blocked tickets resolved and load/chaos tests green for two consecutive runs.
out_of_scope: Large-scale server re-architecting (server-side kernel changes) — this ticket only defines the client contract and cutover controls.
Automatic model-level fallback logic (e.g., swap to cheaper model variant) — handled by routing policies team.
SDK language bindings other than Python/TypeScript/Go (will be scheduled separately).
Automatic client-side token encryption key rotation (recommendations will be in docs but implementation is out-of-scope).
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (Canary): Implement SDK feature-flag default=off. Ship to internal canary orgs + 3 external beta partners. Monitor metrics for 72 hours.
Phase 2 (Limited rollout): Enable adaptive mode for opt-in customers and for 5% of production traffic under server-side flag. Collect telemetry and customer feedback.
Phase 3 (Broad rollout): Default server-side flag flips to on for new orgs; legacy compatibility remains for existing orgs with deprecation timeline messaging.
Phase 4 (Deprecation): After 6 months of stable telemetry, deprecate legacy-only toggles with documented migration window and bump SDK minor version.
migration_plan: Provide a small 'resume-helper' library in each SDK for persisting tokens (file, local DB, or secret store examples).
Offer a guided migration checklist for customers: capture current pagination tokens, run canary with local traffic, validate resumed streams for a day.
Create a sandbox script that replays production traffic to the canary API to validate resume semantics without impacting production.
Coordinate with Solutions Eng to run 2 pilot migrations for customers with heavy streaming workloads.
Prepare automated compatibility tests that customers can run against their dataset to assert no missing/duplicate events.
monitoring_and_metrics: Resume success rate (per org, per SDK language)
Average page size returned vs requested (histogram)
Retry count distribution for fetch calls
Median and 95th percentile latency for first token and complete page
Number of rollbacks triggered via REDWOOD_SDK_ADAPTIVE_FETCH env or server header
Errors per 10k fetches tagged by cause (token-mismatch, transient-network, server-500)
open_questions: Q1: Resume token format: Should tokens be opaque base64 blobs or structured JSON with explicit offsets? (Tradeoffs: forward-compatibility vs debuggability.)
Q2: Cross-language token portability: Do we require tokens generated by Python to be readable by Go clients for shared-stream scenarios?
Q3: Default retry behavior: conservative (2 retries) or aggressive (5 retries with exponential backoff) for resumable streams?
Q4: Persistence examples: should we ship first-party wrappers for common secret stores (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager)?
Q5: How to grade 'no-duplicate' semantic for partial-ack semantics used by some customers? Do we provide dedupe helpers?
notes: - Proposed api names: fetch_stream (py), fetchStream (ts), FetchStream(ctx) (go). Open to suggestions from SDK leads.
- UX tradeoff: exposing more control increases complexity; default mode should be safe for most customers.
- Compatibility header name proposed: X-Redwood-SDK-Compat (server can set to 'legacy' or 'adaptive').
- Security note: resume tokens should be treated as secrets; docs must clearly recommend encrypted storage.
- Engineering asked for acceptance test harness by 2025-12-10 to unblock integration testing.
